Model Identification in Control Theory:
from input–output data to a model you can trust

System identification is the art and science of building a dynamical model of a plant from measured input–output data. This page teaches the methods (what the problem is, why each idea exists) and the algorithms (least squares, prediction-error, recursive, and subspace methods) that turn raw samples into a model you can hand to a controller. Everything is one self-contained file: the math is typeset live by an embedded MathJax, all fonts are embedded, and it works offline.

1. Why identify a model at all? — the motivation

Every model-based control design — an LQR regulator, a Kalman filter, a model-predictive controller, a state observer — starts from the same premise: we have a mathematical description of the plant, a map from what we do (inputs $u$) to what we observe ($y$) over time. Where does that description come from? Two routes exist:

  • First-principles (white-box) modeling: write conservation laws, Newton's equations, thermodynamics, and derive a differential equation. Powerful when the physics is well understood, but slow to build, expensive to validate, and genuinely impractical for complex plants — a chemical reactor, an aircraft in flight, a lithium-ion battery, a human knee, a data-center cooling loop.
  • Identification (empirical modeling): inject a carefully chosen input signal, record the response, and fit a model to the measurements. The plant itself becomes the oracle. If you can measure it, you can model it — often in hours instead of months.

System identification is the discipline that makes the second route rigorous. It answers three questions in order: what structure should the model have?, how do we compute its parameters from data?, and how do we know it is good enough? This page is organized exactly along those questions. The same toolbox also powers soft sensors (virtual measurements), fault detection, digital twins, and adaptive control — anywhere a model must be (re)built from data.

Takeaway. Identification turns measured data into a dynamical model, making model-based control practical exactly where first-principles modeling is too slow, too uncertain, or infeasible.

2. The identification problem, stated precisely

Let's pin down the object we work with for most of this page: a discrete-time, linear time-invariant (LTI) system, sampled at a fixed period. We write it in transfer-function form using the backward shift operator $q^{-1}$, defined by $q^{-1}u(t) = u(t-1)$:

$$ y(t) \;=\; \underbrace{G(q)\,u(t)}_{\text{plant dynamics}} \;+\; \underbrace{v(t)}_{\text{disturbance}}, \qquad v(t) = H(q)\,e(t), $$

where $u(t)$ is the scalar input at sample $t$, $y(t)$ the scalar output, $e(t)$ is white noise — a sequence of independent, zero-mean random variables with variance $\sigma^2$ (the randomness we cannot predict) — and $G(q)$, $H(q)$ are rational functions of $q^{-1}$. Everything we cannot explain by $u$ is lumped into the disturbance $v(t)$, which itself is shaped by the "noise filter" $H(q)$. If $H(q)=1$, the disturbance is white; if $H(q)$ has dynamics, the disturbance is colored (correlated across time) — a distinction that will drive the whole story of Section 5.

We collect $N$ samples of input and output, and denote this data set

$$ Z^N = \{\, (u(1),y(1)),\, (u(2),y(2)),\, \ldots,\, (u(N),y(N)) \,\}. $$

A model set is a family of candidate models parameterized by a vector $\theta \in \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{M} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{p}$ (here $p$ is the number of parameters — later we also use $p$ for the AIC penalty, same thing):

$$ \mathcal{M}\;=\;\{\, M(\theta) : \theta \in \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{M}\,\}, $$

For example, $M(\theta)$ might be "all second-order transfer functions $G(q; \theta)$ with $\theta$ the four coefficients". The identification problem is then beautifully compact:

The identification problem. Given the data $Z^N$ and a model set $\mathcal{M}$, choose $\hat{\theta}_N \in \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{M}$ — the member of the set that "best" explains $Z^N$ — and verify that $M(\hat{\theta}_N)$ actually describes the plant.

Two remarks before we proceed, because they shape every algorithm below:

  • There is no "true" model inside our set, in general. The plant is a physical object; our model is a deliberate simplification. So identification does not search for "the truth" — it searches for the best member of the chosen family, and the family is our responsibility (that is the structure question).
  • An identified model is only as good as the data. If the input never excited some mode of the plant, no algorithm can estimate the parameters that describe that mode. This is identifiability, the subject of Section 8 — it is a property of the pair (model set, input), not of the estimator alone.

The whole discipline fits into one loop (Figure 1): design an experiment, gather data, choose a structure, estimate parameters, validate; if validation fails, loop back and change the experiment or the structure. This is why real identification projects are iterative, and why the "algorithm" is only one box in the loop.

Where do candidate structures come from? Think of a spectrum of prior knowledge (Figure 2): at one end you trust physics and only estimate a few constants (a white-box model); at the other end you admit ignorance and let a generic model family absorb everything (black-box). In between lies the enormously practical grey-box regime: the structure comes from insight, the numbers from data.

Figure 2 · The knowledge spectrum. Your choice of structure is a statement about how much you trust physics versus data. The arrow bar marks the grey-box regime where control engineers typically live.
Takeaway. Identification is a loop of experiment → structure → estimate → validate; the model set you choose encodes your prior knowledge and bounds what any estimator can achieve.

3. The core idea: prediction-error methods

What makes one candidate model "explain the data better" than another? The answer that organizes almost all of identification is: a model is useful if it predicts. Whatever we will do with the model — simulate, design a controller, run a Kalman filter — we will ask it to forecast the future output from the past. So define the one-step-ahead predictor: the best guess of $y(t)$ using only data up to time $t-1$ and the model $M(\theta)$,

$$ \hat{y}(t \mid t-1; \theta), $$

and the prediction error — the part of the measured output we did not foresee:

$$ \varepsilon(t,\theta) \;=\; y(t) - \hat{y}(t \mid t-1; \theta). $$

If the model were perfect and the disturbance were absent, $\varepsilon$ would be zero. With noise, the prediction error is exactly the unpredictable part — which is why, for a well-chosen model, the prediction error is statistically indistinguishable from white noise (we will exploit that test in Section 9).

The prediction-error method (PEM) chooses the parameter vector that minimizes the average squared prediction error:

$$ \hat{\theta}_N \;=\; \arg\min_{\theta \in \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{M}}\; V_N(\theta), \qquad V_N(\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \varepsilon(t,\theta)^2. $$

Why squared error? Three reasons stack up. (i) Geometry and calculus: the criterion is smooth and, for models linear in $\theta$, quadratic — which gives us closed-form solutions (next section). (ii) Statistics: for Gaussian white noise, minimizing $\sum \varepsilon^2$ is exactly maximum likelihood — the estimate inherits the attractive properties of MLEs: consistency, asymptotic normality, and (asymptotically) minimum variance. (iii) Interpretation: minimizing mean squared prediction error is minimizing forecast variance, which is what a controller or observer ultimately cares about.

Notice what the predictor does that a plain simulation does not (Figure 3): a simulator feeds its own past outputs back into the model, so its error accumulates and even diverges if the model is unstable; the predictor, by contrast, feeds the measured past output back in. Prediction is therefore always well-behaved — an unstable plant can still have a perfectly stable one-step predictor — and it uses strictly more information than simulation does.

Figure 3 · Predictor versus simulator. The predictor closes the loop with measured past outputs (dashed blue lines), so the prediction error $\varepsilon$ stays honest even for unstable plants; a simulator closes its loop with its own past outputs (orange box) and drifts. PEM optimizes the predictor.

Why is the predictor itself a model output rather than a free design choice? For a given model $M(\theta) = (G(q,\theta), H(q,\theta))$ the statistically optimal one-step predictor is fixed — it is the conditional expectation of $y(t)$ given the past, which for LTI systems with rational $H$ has a neat closed form. We will meet its concrete instances in Section 5 (the model structures), but the shape of the machinery — pick a model set, derive its predictor, minimize squared prediction error — is the skeleton of PEM, and least squares (next section) is simply the special case where the predictor is linear in the parameters.

Takeaway. The prediction-error method is the organizing principle of identification: choose $\theta$ to make the model's one-step forecasts as accurate as possible — everything else (least squares, recursive and subspace algorithms) is a computational or structural specialization of this idea.

4. The workhorse: ARX models and least squares

Start with the simplest model structure that captures dynamics, the ARX model (Auto-Regressive with eXogenous input). It is a difference equation with a white-noise disturbance entering directly:

$$ A(q)\,y(t) \;=\; B(q)\,u(t) + e(t), \qquad \begin{aligned} A(q) &= 1 + a_1 q^{-1} + \cdots + a_{n_a} q^{-n_a},\\ B(q) &= b_1 q^{-1} + b_2 q^{-2} + \cdots + b_{n_b} q^{-n_b}, \end{aligned} $$

with orders $n_a, n_b$ chosen by the user. Expanding and rearranging, the output regresses on its own past and on the past input:

$$ y(t) = -a_1 y(t-1) - \cdots - a_{n_a} y(t-n_a) + b_1 u(t-1) + \cdots + b_{n_b} u(t-n_b) \;+\; e(t). $$

Collect the regressors and the parameters into vectors — this is the crucial trick, because $y(t)$ is now linear in the unknown vector $\theta$:

$$ y(t) = \varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}} \theta + e(t), \qquad \begin{aligned} \varphi(t) &= \big[\,{-}y(t-1),\ldots, -y(t-n_a),\; u(t-1),\ldots, u(t-n_b)\,\big]^{\mathsf{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p},\\[2pt] \theta &= \big[\,a_1,\ldots,a_{n_a},\; b_1,\ldots,b_{n_b}\,\big]^{\mathsf{T}}, \qquad p = n_a + n_b. \end{aligned} $$

Note the minus signs: we put the $y$-terms on the left as $-a_i y(t-i)$, so they appear in the regression vector as $-y(t-i)$. Why bother? Because now least squares becomes a linear algebra problem. Stack all $N$ equations, one per time sample, into one matrix equation:

$$ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} y(1) \\ y(2) \\ \vdots \\ y(N) \end{bmatrix}}_{Y\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{N}} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \varphi(1)^{\mathsf{T}} \\ \varphi(2)^{\mathsf{T}} \\ \vdots \\ \varphi(N)^{\mathsf{T}} \end{bmatrix}}_{\Phi\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{N\times p}} \, \theta \;+\; \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} e(1) \\ e(2) \\ \vdots \\ e(N) \end{bmatrix}}_{E}, \qquad Y = \Phi\theta + E. $$

The least-squares (LS) estimate minimizes the sum of squared residuals over all $\theta$:

$$ \hat{\theta}_N \;=\; \arg\min_{\theta}\ \big\| Y - \Phi\theta \big\|^2 \;=\; \big(\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi\big)^{-1} \Phi^{\mathsf{T}} Y, $$

assuming the $p\times p$ matrix $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi$ is invertible (the identifiability condition — Section 8 says exactly what input makes this true). Why this formula? It is the solution of the normal equations $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi\,\theta = \Phi^{\mathsf{T}}Y$, obtained by setting the gradient of the quadratic $\|Y-\Phi\theta\|^2 = Y^{\mathsf{T}}Y - 2\theta^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}Y + \theta^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi\theta$ to zero. Because the criterion is a convex parabola in $\theta$ (the matrix $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi$ is positive semidefinite by construction), that stationary point is the global minimum — no iteration, no local minima, one shot.

The geometry explains the formula. Think of $Y$ as a vector in $N$-dimensional space (one dimension per sample). The matrix $\Phi$ has $p \le N$ columns, so $\{\Phi\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}^p\}$ is a $p$-dimensional subspace — the set of all perfectly explainable outputs. We want the point of that subspace closest to $Y$; "closest" in Euclidean distance is the orthogonal projection (Figure 4). The residual $\hat{E} = Y - \Phi\hat\theta_N$ is therefore perpendicular to every column of $\Phi$: $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\hat E = 0$, which is the normal equation. The formula $\hat\theta_N = (\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}Y$ is just the projection expressed in coordinates.

$\hat E = Y - \Phi\hat\theta_N$

Figure 4 · Least squares as projection. $\hat\theta_N$ positions $\Phi\hat\theta_N$ at the foot of the perpendicular from $Y$ to the model's reachable subspace; the residual is orthogonal to all regressors. This picture is why $\hat\theta_N = (\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}Y$.

Why trust this estimate? Three classical statistical results pin down when LS is good, and each has a one-line "why":

  • Unbiasedness & consistency. If the noise $e(t)$ is zero-mean white and independent of the input, then $\mathbb{E}[\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}E] = 0$ in the normal equations, so $\mathbb{E}\,\hat\theta_N = \theta$ and $\hat\theta_N \to \theta$ as $N\to\infty$ (averaging kills the noise).
  • Gauss–Markov optimality. Among all linear unbiased estimators, LS has the smallest covariance: $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\theta_N) = \sigma^2 (\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi)^{-1}$ (with $\sigma^2$ the noise variance). No other linear, unbiased method beats it — this is why the formula's inverse appears: it is the covariance structure of the problem itself.
  • Consistency needs excitation. The estimate converges only if $\tfrac{1}{N}\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi \to \mathbb{E}[\varphi(t)\varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}]$ is nonsingular — i.e. the input must make the regressors linearly independent "on average". That is the persistent-excitation condition, Section 8.

Worked example: a first-order ARX fit by hand

Let's make this concrete with four noise-free samples of a first-order plant $y(t) = 0.5\,y(t-1) + 1.0\,u(t-1)$, i.e. $n_a = n_b = 1$, true $\theta^\star = (0.5, 1.0)$. Choose input $u(0)=1,\ u(1)=-1,\ u(2)=2,\ u(3)=-1$ and initial condition $y(0)=1$, then the recurrence gives $y(1)=1.5,\ y(2)=-0.25,\ y(3)=1.875,\ y(4)=-0.0625$. Stacking rows $t=1,\ldots,4$ with regression vector $\varphi(t) = [y(t-1),\ u(t-1)]^{\mathsf{T}}$:

$t$$u(t-1)$$y(t-1)$$y(t)$$\varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}$
1111.5$(1,\ 1)$
2−11.5−0.25$(1.5,\ -1)$
32−0.251.875$(-0.25,\ 2)$
4−11.875−0.0625$(1.875,\ -1)$

Then the normal-equation ingredients — each entry is a sum over the four rows — and their solution are:

$$ \Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 6.828 & -2.875 \\ -2.875 & 7.000 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Phi^{\mathsf{T}}Y = \begin{bmatrix} 0.539 \\ 5.563 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \hat\theta = \begin{bmatrix} 0.500 \\ 1.000 \end{bmatrix}, $$

exactly the true parameters — as promised for the noise-free case. With noise, $\hat\theta$ would scatter around $(0.5, 1.0)$ with covariance $\sigma^2(\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi)^{-1}$; more data shrinks the scatter like $1/\sqrt{N}$. (Keep the numbers in sight when you play with the live demo in Section 11: it is this same computation, scaled up.)

Takeaway. For ARX models with white noise, least squares is a single closed-form matrix operation that is unbiased, consistent, Gauss–Markov optimal, and geometrically a projection — the cleanest possible identification algorithm.

5. When least squares fails: colored noise, bias, and the general PEM

Section 4's elegance rests on one assumption: the disturbance entering the ARX equation is white. Real plants violate this constantly. Sensor noise, unmeasured disturbances, and load changes arrive after the dynamics, so the true structure is closer to

$$ y(t) \;=\; \varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}\theta \;+\; v(t), $$

with $v(t)$ a colored (time-correlated) noise, e.g. $v(t) = \tfrac{1}{1-0.7q^{-1}}\,e(t)$. The regression vector $\varphi(t)$ contains past outputs $y(t-1),\ldots$ — but each past output contains its own past noise, and colored noise persists across time. Hence $\varphi(t)$ and $v(t)$ are correlated: $\mathbb{E}[\varphi(t)\,v(t)] \neq 0$. Substitute $Y = \Phi\theta + V$ into the LS formula and take expectations (as $N\to\infty$):

$$ \hat\theta_N \;\to\; \theta^\star \;+\; \Big(\mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(t)\varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}\big]\Big)^{-1} \,\mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(t)\,v(t)\big] \;\neq\; \theta^\star . $$

There is the bias: a systematic error proportional to the noise–regressor correlation $\mathbb{E}[\varphi v]$. Least squares is not estimating the plant; it is estimating "plant plus whatever leaks through the correlation". Figure 5 shows why: the criterion surface that LS actually minimizes is a shifted version of the ideal one — its bottom sits at the biased $\hat\theta$ rather than at the truth $\theta^\star$.

ideal cost: minimum at the true $\theta^\star$
cost LS actually minimizes: min at $\hat\theta$
bias: $\left[\mathbb{E}\,\varphi\varphi^{\mathsf{T}}\right]^{-1}\mathbb{E}\,\varphi v$
why: $\varphi(t)$ (past $y$) correlates with colored $v(t)$
scatter of $\varphi(t)$ vs $v(t)$: sloped cloud ⇒ nonzero $\mathbb{E}[\varphi v]$
Figure 5 · The bias mechanism. When the disturbance is colored, the regressors $\varphi(t)$ (which contain past outputs) correlate with the noise; the criterion LS minimizes (dashed) is a systematically displaced version of the ideal one (solid), so the estimate converges to the wrong parameters.

Two families of remedies exist, and both show up throughout the field. Instrumental-variable (IV) methods swap the regressors for proxies; general PEM models the noise itself. Let's take IV first because it is one line, then PEM because it is the deep answer.

Remedy 1 — Instrumental variables: replace the correlated regressor

The bias term is caused by $\mathbb{E}[\varphi v] \neq 0$. If we could multiply the equation by a vector $\zeta(t)$ that is correlated with the regressors but uncorrelated with the noise, the noise term would average out. That is the instrument. The IV estimate is

$$ \hat\theta_N^{\mathrm{IV}} \;=\; \big(\underbrace{\Psi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi}_{\text{instruments × regressors}}\big)^{-1} \underbrace{\Psi^{\mathsf{T}}Y}_{\text{instruments × data}}, \qquad \Psi = \begin{bmatrix} \zeta(1)^{\mathsf{T}} \\ \vdots \\ \zeta(N)^{\mathsf{T}} \end{bmatrix}, $$

with $\zeta(t)$ chosen so that $\mathbb{E}[\zeta(t)\,v(t)] = 0$ (noise-blindness) while $\tfrac{1}{N}\Psi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi$ stays nonsingular (still enough information). In the old normal equation the noise term was $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}V$; now it is $\Psi^{\mathsf{T}}V$, and its expectation vanishes. Why would LS work at all then? Because when the noise is white, choosing $\zeta = \varphi$ makes IV exactly LS — LS is the special case where the regressors are their own valid instruments.

  • A classic instrument: for an OE structure, delayed inputs $\zeta(t) = [u(t-1-k),\ldots]^{\mathsf{T}}$ are noise-free by construction (input is known!) and correlate with $\varphi(t)$ through the plant dynamics.
  • The price: you traded bias for variance. IV is consistent but not Gauss–Markov; it wastes information and needs a good instrument, which in practice means knowing roughly where the dynamics are.

Remedy 2 — General PEM: model the noise, don't dodge it

The deep fix is to parameterize both the plant and the noise filter and estimate them together. Then the predictor (Section 3) filters out the correlation by construction. The standard families, ordered by how the disturbance enters (Figure 6):

$$ \begin{array}{ll} \textbf{ARX:} & A(q)\,y(t) = B(q)\,u(t) + e(t) \\[2pt] \textbf{ARMAX:} & A(q)\,y(t) = B(q)\,u(t) + C(q)\,e(t) \\[2pt] \textbf{OE:} & y(t) = \dfrac{B(q)}{F(q)}\,u(t) + e(t) \\[2pt] \textbf{BJ:} & y(t) = \dfrac{B(q)}{F(q)}\,u(t) + \dfrac{C(q)}{D(q)}\,e(t) \end{array} $$

Figure 6 · The four standard model structures. Each row shows where the white noise $e(t)$ is injected relative to the plant filters $A, B, C, D, F$. ARX lets the noise pass through $1/A$ (so LS is biased when the true noise is colored, recall Figure 5); OE keeps the noise purely additive (white); ARMAX and BJ give the noise its own filter $C(q)$, letting the estimator "whiten" the disturbance.

Each structure induces its own one-step predictor (from Section 3's recipe, $\hat y = H^{-1} G u + (1-H^{-1}) y$):

$$ \begin{array}{ll} \textbf{ARX:} & \hat y = \dfrac{B}{A}\,u + \Big(1 - \dfrac{1}{A}\Big) y \qquad (\text{linear in } \theta \Rightarrow \text{closed form, §4}) \\[4pt] \textbf{ARMAX:} & \hat y = \dfrac{B}{C}\,u + \Big(1 - \dfrac{A}{C}\Big) y \\[4pt] \textbf{OE:} & \hat y = \dfrac{B}{F}\,u \\[4pt] \textbf{BJ:} & \hat y = \dfrac{D}{C}\,\dfrac{B}{F}\,u + \Big(1 - \dfrac{D}{C}\Big) y \end{array} $$

The predictors for ARMAX, OE and BJ are nonlinear in $\theta$ (parameters appear in denominators), so we cannot solve the PEM criterion in closed form. Instead we iterate — the standard algorithm is Gauss–Newton: linearize the predictor about the current guess and take a damped step,

$$ \theta^{(k+1)} \;=\; \theta^{(k)} \;-\; \Big[\,V_N''(\theta^{(k)})\,\Big]^{-1} V_N'(\theta^{(k)}), \qquad V_N' = -\frac{2}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \varepsilon(t,\theta)\,\psi(t,\theta), $$

where $\psi(t,\theta) = \tfrac{\partial \hat y}{\partial \theta}$ is the gradient of the predictor, and the Hessian is approximated by $\tfrac{2}{N}\sum \psi \psi^{\mathsf{T}} \succeq 0$ (a Gauss–Newton, not full Newton, choice: it stays positive semi-definite and ignores curvature of $\varepsilon$ itself). The beautiful part: those gradients are themselves filtered regression vectors. For ARMAX, for instance, $\psi(t) = \tfrac{1}{C(q)}\,\big[-y(t-1),\ldots,\ u(t-1),\ldots,\ -\varepsilon(t-1),\ldots\big]^{\mathsf{T}}$: the very same regressors as in §4, but passed through $1/C(q)$ and with lagged prediction errors in place of the noise. So PEM is "least squares on filtered regressors, iterated" — Section 4 reappears inside the loop. One iteration from a good start already removes most of the bias.

Why the noise model is a design choice, not a fact. You rarely believe $C(q)$ describes the "true" disturbance; you choose it so that the modeled residual is approximately white. A richer noise model (and a richer plant) lets the estimator chase more of the signal, but costs variance. This bias–variance trade-off recurs in Section 9.
Takeaway. Colored noise correlates with the regressors and biases least squares; IV removes the correlation by instrumenting the regressors, while general PEM (ARMAX/OE/BJ) removes it by modeling and filtering the noise — losing the closed form but gaining consistency, at the price of an iterative Gauss–Newton search.

6. Online identification: recursive least squares (RLS)

Batch least squares needs all $N$ samples at once. Three real-world pressures push us to a recursive version that updates the estimate sample by sample: (i) the plant drifts (aging actuators, temperature swings) and we want to track it; (ii) storage and latency — sensors stream, controllers must act now; (iii) adaptive control — identify and redesign the controller every sample, the "self-tuning regulator" idea.

RLS is not an approximation of LS; it computes exactly the same answer at every time $t$ as a batch fit over all data seen so far, but with a constant per-step cost. The derivation is one algebraic identity: write the batch solution at time $t$ in terms of the solution at $t-1$ and the new sample $(u(t), y(t))$, then apply the matrix inversion lemma to avoid inverting $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi$ afresh. Let $\varepsilon(t)$ be the prediction error of the previous estimate against the new sample, and $P(t) = (\Phi_t^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi_t)^{-1}$ the "information inverse" (later interpretable as a covariance). The update is:

$$ \begin{aligned} \varepsilon(t) &= y(t) - \varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}\hat\theta(t-1) && \text{(prediction error on the new sample)}\\[2pt] K(t) &= \frac{P(t-1)\,\varphi(t)}{1 + \varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}} P(t-1)\,\varphi(t)} && \text{(gain vector)}\\[2pt] \hat\theta(t) &= \hat\theta(t-1) + K(t)\,\varepsilon(t) && \text{(correction = gain × error)}\\[2pt] P(t) &= \big(I - K(t)\,\varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}\big) P(t-1) && \text{(covariance update)} \end{aligned} $$

Read the structure aloud and it makes complete sense: new estimate = old estimate + gain × how wrong the old estimate just was. The gain $K(t)$ is a vector in parameter space that says "the new sample mostly corrects these directions, not those" — it is large along directions where the information matrix $P^{-1}$ is weak. The scalar denominator $1 + \varphi^{\mathsf{T}}P\varphi$ normalizes by the uncertainty of the prediction itself. This is precisely the Kalman filter update, specialized to a static parameter ($\theta(t+1) = \theta(t)$): RLS is the Kalman filter for the "constant state" $\theta$, with $P(t) = \operatorname{cov}(\hat\theta(t))$.

Self-tuning regulator: identify and redesign the controller every sample while the plant runs.
Forgetting factor $\lambda$: $(I-K\varphi^{\mathsf{T}})P/\lambda$; old data decays geometrically, $\lambda<1$ enables tracking.
Figure 7 · The recursive least-squares loop. Each sample produces a prediction, an error, a gain, and a correction; the new $\hat\theta(t)$ feeds the next prediction (dashed feedback) and, in adaptive control, the online controller design.

Tracking a drifting plant: the forgetting factor. The covariance update as written keeps accumulating all past information, so after long runs $P(t) \to 0$ and the estimate freezes, no longer able to follow changes. The fix is to discount old samples exponentially by a forgetting factor $0 \ll \lambda \le 1$:

$$ K(t) \;=\; \frac{P(t-1)\,\varphi(t)}{\lambda + \varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}} P(t-1)\,\varphi(t)}, \qquad P(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{\lambda}\big(I - K(t)\varphi(t)^{\mathsf{T}}\big)P(t-1), $$

which is equivalent to minimizing $\sum_{k=1}^{t} \lambda^{t-k}\varepsilon(k)^2$ — recent samples weigh $\lambda^{-j}$ more. The price of tracking is variance: with $\lambda < 1$ the effective data window is only $1/(1-\lambda)$ samples, so the estimate jitters. Do not forget (pun intended): $\lambda$ is the online counterpart of "how much data do you believe" that we will meet again as model-order selection in Section 9.

RLS is the algorithmic seed of a whole family: RELS (recursive extended least squares) and the recursive prediction-error methods (RPEM) generalize it to ARMAX by including lagged prediction errors in the regression vector — exactly the filtered-regressor idea of Section 5, now online. Every adaptive controller since the 1970s self-tuning regulator ([Åström & Wittenmark], §10) owes its existence to this loop.

Takeaway. RLS reproduces batch least squares sample-by-sample with a constant-time update — a Kalman filter on the static parameter $\theta$ — and the forgetting factor $\lambda$ trades tracking speed against estimate variance, making identification a closed loop around a drifting plant.

7. Black-box state-space: subspace identification (N4SID, MOESP)

PEM from Section 5 is statistically beautiful but computationally and structurally demanding: you choose a model family, orders, and a noise model; then you run a nonlinear search that can stall in local minima — and everything scales badly to multi-input multi-output (MIMO) plants, where the parameterization choices multiply. Subspace methods answer with a radically different strategy: go straight from the raw data to a state-space model using linear algebra only — no user-chosen noise model, no iteration, no parameterization. The price is some statistical efficiency (they are consistent but not minimum-variance in general), which practice happily pays for robustness.

First, recall what a state-space model is — at every sample $t$ the plant has a compact summary, the state $x(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, from which the future unfolds linearly:

$$ x(t+1) = A\,x(t) + B\,u(t), \qquad y(t) = C\,x(t) + D\,u(t) + \text{noise}, $$

with system matrices $A$ ($n\times n$), $B$, $C$, $D$. If we knew $A,B,C,D$, everything downstream (Kalman filter, MPC, LQG) is standard. Subspace identification's task: recover $A,B,C,D$ (and, roughly, the order $n$) directly from the data blocks.

The key structural fact. Stack the future outputs into a block-Hankel matrix -- rows are successive time shifts of the measurements, columns are different starting times:

$$ Y_f = O_i\,X_f + H_i\,U_f + \text{noise}, \qquad O_i = \begin{bmatrix} C \\ CA \\ \vdots \\ CA^{\,i-1} \end{bmatrix} \quad (\text{extended observability matrix}), $$

i.e. the future-output matrix $Y_f$ lives in the row space of the inputs $U_f$ plus the column space of the observability matrix $O_i$, driven by the (unknown) state matrix $X_f$. If we could remove the input contribution, the remaining part would live exactly in $\operatorname{range}(O_i)$ — and $O_i$ contains $A$ and $C$ by construction. That removal is a projection (an oblique one, along the row space of $U_f$ onto the past-data space $W_p = [U_p;\ Y_p]$):

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{O}} \;=\; Y_f\,/_{U_f}\; W_p \;=\; O_i\,X_f \quad(\text{up to noise}). $$

Then one singular value decomposition (SVD) reveals both the order and the matrices (Figure 8): the number of "large" singular values of $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}$ is the state dimension $n$ (the rest are noise-floor), the left singular vectors give $O_i$ up to a similarity transform, and $A, C$ fall out of $O_i$'s shift-invariance: dropping the first/last block rows of $O_i$ and solving a least-squares problem yields $A$; $C$ is just the first block row. Finally $B, D$ are estimated by one more least-squares step on the state equation with the reconstructed states. Two famous algorithms instantiate this skeleton — N4SID (van Overschee & De Moor 1994, combined deterministic–stochastic by using both past input and output as instruments) and MOESP (Verhaegen, based on an LQ factorization that decouples the input before the SVD); they share the projection-then-SVD core and differ in how the projections are computed and combined.

Figure 8 · Subspace identification in three moves. (1) Build block-Hankel matrices from the raw data; project the future outputs away from the future inputs onto past data — what remains lives in the observability range. (2) The SVD scree plot shows the model order as a gap between signal and noise singular values. (3) Shift-invariance of $O_i$ yields $A, C$; one last least-squares yields $B, D$. No nonlinear search anywhere.

Why the SVD is the right tool here. The SVD of a matrix is the canonical way to separate a low-rank "signal" from a "noise" part: the rank of the noiseless $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}$ is exactly $n$ (its columns span $\operatorname{range} O_i$), and noise inflates the smaller singular values. Looking at the scree plot and choosing $n$ where the values plateau is the subspace analogue of choosing the order $n_a, n_b$ in Section 4 — we will formalize both choices in Section 9. This is also the modern, data-driven heir of the classical Ho–Kalman realization theorem (1966), which recovered a minimal state-space realization from the impulse response: subspace methods recover it from input–output data in one shot (the impulse response is conceptually the special case of a suitable input).

What you give up. Subspace estimates are consistent under mild conditions (persistently exciting inputs, mild noise assumptions — roughly Section 8's conditions) but they are not maximum likelihood: the projection throws away the fine noise structure that PEM exploits, so for small samples and very precise noise models PEM wins. In return you get a numerically robust, MIMO-native, iteration-free black-box route to exactly the $(A,B,C,D)$ that Kalman filtering and MPC want. The modern data-driven methods (e.g. data-enabled predictive control) push this "model-free from data" philosophy one step further by applying subspace-style projections directly in the controller — Section 10's outlook.

Takeaway. Subspace identification replaces structure choice and nonlinear search with linear algebra — block-Hankel projection plus one SVD, whose singular-value gap picks the order — yielding balanced state-space models directly from data, ideal for MIMO plants and for feeding Kalman filters and MPC.

8. What makes identification possible: identifiability and experiment design

Every algorithm so far assumed the numbers can be extracted — that the normal matrix $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi$ is invertible, that the excitation "reaches" the dynamics. That is not free: it is a contract between the model structure and the input signal, and when the contract is violated no estimator can help. Two distinct notions are usually conflated under "identifiability" (Ljung makes the split explicit):

  • Structural (theoretical) identifiability — a property of the model set alone: is the map $\theta \mapsto M(\theta)$ one-to-one on $\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{M}$? If two different parameter vectors give the same input–output behavior, the data can never tell them apart, whatever you measure. Example: an ARX model with $B(q)$ and $A(q)$ sharing a common factor — the pole-zero pair cancels, and infinitely many $(\theta)$ produce the same transfer function. The fix is a coprime (or otherwise minimal) parameterization.
  • Practical (data-dependent) identifiability — a property of the pair (model set, data): does $Z^N$ contain enough information to distinguish the candidates? This is where persistent excitation (PE) enters: the input must be rich enough that the regressors $(\varphi(t))$ become linearly independent "on average", i.e. $\tfrac{1}{N}\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi \to \mathbb{E}[\varphi \varphi^{\mathsf{T}}]$ nonsingular.

Persistent excitation in one line: a scalar signal is persistently exciting of order $n$ when, in the limit, the empirical autocorrelation matrix built from $n$ consecutive samples is nonsingular — roughly, its spectrum is nonzero at at least $n$ frequencies. Consequences for inputs (Figure 9):

  • Sinusesoid: spectral density = two lines $\pm\omega_0$; PE of order 2 only — enough for a first-order plant, hopeless for a third-order one.
  • PRBS (pseudo-random binary sequence, a deterministic long-period two-level signal): flat spectrum up to a cut-off set by its clock rate — PE of order up to its length minus one, and the standard industrial workhorse because it is also easy to generate and safe (bounded amplitudes).
  • Chirp / multisine: deliberately sweep or stack frequencies across the plant's bandwidth — ideal when you already know roughly where the dynamics live.
  • White noise: theoretically PE of every order (flat spectrum), but unbounded amplitude ⇒ not implementable and wasteful; PRBS is its practical, bounded sibling.
$$ \text{input }u \text{ has } \mathrm{PE}(n) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \begin{bmatrix} u(t) \\ \vdots \\ u(t-n+1) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u(t) & \cdots & u(t-n+1) \end{bmatrix} \succ 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \Phi_u(\omega) > 0 \text{ at } \ge n \text{ frequencies}. $$
sine — one frequency
time trace: $u(t)$
spectrum: 2 lines ⇒ $\mathrm{PE}(2)$
PRBS — flat spectrum, many frequencies
time trace: $u(t)=\pm 1$
spectrum: flat ⇒ high PE order
plant bandwidth inside the flat region; sample fast enough to see the dynamics
Figure 9 · Persistent excitation. A sine excites exactly one frequency (PE order 2); a PRBS excites everything below its clock frequency with a flat spectrum, which is why it — and its cousins (chirps, multisines, filtered white noise) — are the standard identification inputs. You get to estimate exactly the modes the input can reach.

Practical rules of thumb follow directly. For an ARX model, the regressors span $p = n_a + n_b$ directions, so $\mathrm{PE}(n_a + n_b)$ is the ticket to a nonsingular normal matrix; OE-type structures need roughly order $2n$ (effectively you must excite enough to separate plant poles from noise-model poles); and in closed-loop identification the feedback correlation makes things subtler — the input spectrum is shaped by the controller, and standard open-loop conditions fail (one needs direct/indirect or joint input–output variants). Sampling must be faster than the fastest relevant dynamics (anti-aliasing first!), and long enough that the averages in the PE condition actually converge — the estimate's covariance shrinks only like $\sigma^2/N$, so there is no shortcut around collecting data.

Why all this matters for the "algorithm" question. Unidentifiability shows up as a singular or ill-conditioned $\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi$: the estimate blows up along the unexcited directions. A good identification run spends as much effort on the input as on the estimator — the data contract comes first.
Takeaway. Identifiability is a joint property of model structure and input signal: structural redundancy (common factors, over-parameterization) must be avoided by modeling, and persistent excitation — a rich-enough input spectrum over the plant's bandwidth — must be engineered, because no algorithm can estimate modes the data never activated.

9. Did we get a good model? Validation and order selection

Estimation is only half the loop (Figure 1). The other half asks the uncomfortable question: would this model fool us on data it has never seen? Three complementary guards exist, and skipping any of them is how confident but wrong models get shipped.

Guard 1 — Residual analysis: the model's leftover should be noise

If the model captured the plant and the noise model captured the disturbance, the one-step prediction errors $\hat\varepsilon(t) = y(t) - \hat y(t \mid t-1; \hat\theta_N)$ should be unpredictable — that is, white. Test this statistically with the sample autocorrelation of the residuals and their cross-correlation with the input (valuable beyond $\tau=0$: residual energy at lag $\tau$ vs $u$ means a missed input path):

$$ \hat\rho(\tau) \;=\; \frac{\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_t \hat\varepsilon(t)\,\hat\varepsilon(t-\tau)} {\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_t \hat\varepsilon(t)^2}, \qquad \text{white noise passes iff } |\hat\rho(\tau)| \le \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{N}} \ \text{for all } \tau \ne 0, $$

intuitively: if any lag sticks out of the band $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}$, there is still a predictable pattern in the residuals — a systematic dynamics or noise-model flaw — and the model is incomplete (Figure 11, right). Exactly the residual shapes we can fix: colored residual with structure $\Rightarrow$ add dynamics or a noise model; residual correlated with $u$ $\Rightarrow$ missing input path.

Guard 2 — Cross-validation: the honest test on fresh data

Residual analysis uses the same data the model was fitted on, so it can be fooled by overfitting (Section 10's bias–variance picture). The honest benchmark is to split the data: fit on the training part, then evaluate prediction error on the validation part (or use an entirely fresh experiment). If the model predicts unseen data about as well as it predicts the training data, it has learned dynamics — not memorized samples. This is the same held-out instinct modern machine learning uses; identification papers call it "cross-validation" or "fresh-data validation". For parametric fits the leave-one-out and $k$-fold variants are the common incarnations.

Guard 3 — Complexity control: orders, AIC/BIC, and the bias–variance trade-off

More parameters always reduce the training error (the criterion $V_N$ can only decrease as the model family grows) but add variance: the estimate becomes sensitive to the specific noise realization, and generalization degrades. Figure 10 shows the canonical picture: training error falls monotonically with complexity $p$; validation error is U-shaped, initially falling as we remove bias (undershooting), later rising as variance takes over (overshooting).

Figure 11 · The whiteness test. Residual autocorrelation confined to the $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}$ band means nothing predictable is left. A lag that sticks out of the band means the model missed dynamics — upgrade it and refit.

When you cannot afford hold-out data (small $N$), information criteria approximate validation from the fit itself. The Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC) both penalize the minimum criterion value by the number of parameters $p$ (which equals $n_a + n_b + \ldots$ for PEM structures):

$$ \mathrm{AIC} = N \log V_N(\hat\theta_N) + 2p, \qquad \mathrm{BIC} = N \log V_N(\hat\theta_N) + p \log N, $$

and you pick the model minimizing the criterion. Why these formulas? AIC stems from the asymptotic likelihood (Section 3's MLE view): $N\log V_N$ is essentially minus twice the log-likelihood, and $2p$ is the expected overfitting penalty under asymptotics; BIC adds the stiffer $p\log N$ penalty, trading some fit for guaranteed consistency as $N$ grows. Neither replaces validation — they are cheap proxies that encode the same U-curve of Figure 10 into one number. For subspace identification, the same selection question is answered by the SVD gap (Figure 8): order $n$ = number of singular values above the noise floor.

One more layer completes the story: uncertainty. A point estimate $\hat\theta_N$ without a covariance is a promise without a warranty — the PEM covariance $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\theta_N) \approx \tfrac{\sigma^2}{N} \left[\tfrac{1}{N}\sum \psi \psi^{\mathsf{T}}\right]^{-1}$ (with $\psi$ of Section 5) propagates directly into controller-design margins, robust stability certificates, and Kalman-filter tuning.

Takeaway. A model earns trust only on data it has not seen: residual whiteness checks the leftovers for predictability, cross-validation measures generalization, and AIC/BIC or the SVD gap automate the complexity choice — together they turn "fitted" into "validated".

10. Where this fits: one toolbox, many hats

Step back and you see that "identification" is not a separate little corner of control theory — it is the same statistical machinery that appears everywhere in estimation, wearing different hats:

  • PEM is maximum likelihood for dynamic models. Section 5's Gauss–Newton on prediction errors is the parameter-estimation analogue of the Kalman filter being the state-estimation analogue: both minimize a prediction-error variance, one over a static parameter, the other over a dynamic state. RLS (Section 6) is literally a Kalman filter for the constant state $\theta$.
  • Least squares is linear regression. Section 4's formula is exactly the one-machine-learning-101 linear regression; PEM is nonlinear least squares; RLS is online/streaming regression; the Gauss–Newton curvature $\sum\psi\psi^{\mathsf{T}}$ is the Fisher information. Validation (Section 9) is supervised-learning's held-out evaluation; AIC/BIC are its complexity penalties. If you know one field, you know the skeleton of the other — identification just specializes the regressors to delayed signals (dynamics) and cares about which noise structure creates bias (Sections 4–5).
  • Subspace methods are data-driven realization theory. The Ho–Kalman theorem (impulse response → minimal realization) is the ancestor of N4SID/MOESP (data blocks → $(A,B,C,D)$); both owe their success to the SVD's rank -revealing property. The modern data-driven control line (DeePC and friends) pushes the same projection philosophy onto the controller itself, skipping the model entirely.
  • Experiment design is design of experiments. Persistence of excitation (Section 8) is the dynamic-systems version of "which measurements to take and with which inputs" — the same D-optimality instincts used in statistics and chemometrics.

Three horizons are worth knowing about before you leave: nonlinear identification (grey-box with physics, NARX/NARMAX models, neural state-space models, operator-Koopman lifting — same PEM criterion, harder optimization), closed-loop identification (identify under feedback, e.g. while an existing controller runs — the correlation calculus of Section 5 reappears and requires specialized methods), and robust/uncertainty-aware design (propagate $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\theta_N)$ into control design, robust controllers against the identified model class). The toolbox below is the load-bearing foundation of all of them: predict → fit → validate, then decide what to measure next.

Takeaway. Identification is estimation with dynamics: the same least-squares, maximum-likelihood, recursive and projection ideas that power regression, Kalman filtering and realization theory — and the same validation discipline machine learning preaches — specialized to delayed regressors, noise models, and the question "what must my input excite?"

11. Live demo: fit an ARX model, watch bias appear

This widget simulates a second-order plant and fits an ARX(2,2) model to its input–output data with the batch least-squares formula of Section 4 — exactly the computation of the worked example, scaled up. For readability the model is written in the direct difference-equation convention $y(t)=a_1 y(t-1)+a_2 y(t-2)+b_1 u(t-1)+b_2 u(t-2)+e(t)$ (the same ARX as $A(q)y(t)=B(q)u(t)+e(t)$ with $A(q)=1-a_1q^{-1}-a_2q^{-2}$). Two switches make the story visible:

  • Noise: white vs colored. With white noise the least-squares estimates sit on the truth (Section 4's consistency). Toggle to colored noise (an AR(1) disturbance) and the parameters drift away from the truth — the bias of Section 5, live. This widget illustrates the mechanism; it does not prove it.
  • Noise level $\sigma$ and data length $N$. Watch the scatter of the estimates shrink with $1/\sqrt{N}$ (more data) and grow with $\sigma$ (more noise), exactly as the covariance formula $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\theta) = \sigma^2(\Phi^{\mathsf{T}}\Phi)^{-1}$ predicts.

Further reading

  • L. Ljung, System Identification: Theory for the User, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 1999 — the standard reference; the whole arc of this page (PEM, model structures, identifiability, validation) is its core.
  • T. Söderström & P. Stoica, System Identification, Prentice Hall, 1989 — rigorous, heavily algorithmic; excellent on IV and PE conditions.
  • K. J. Åström & B. Wittenmark, Adaptive Control, 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1995 — RLS and the self-tuning regulator in context.
  • M. Verhaegen & V. Verdult, Filtering and System Identification: A Least Squares Approach, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2007 — subspace methods (MOESP) presented cleanly.
  • P. van Overschee & B. De Moor, Subspace Identification for Linear Systems, Kluwer, 1996 — N4SID in depth.
  • UCB ME233 lecture notes (Xu Chen) — RLS derivations with the matrix inversion lemma.
  • System Identification and Recursive Least Squares (Xu Chen) — compact primer.
  • PySIB: an open-source Python toolbox for linear system identification — implement all of the above in a few lines.

One-paragraph summary (if the page were a sentence)

Identification turns input–output data into a model by (1) choosing a model set that encodes how much physics you trust, (2) minimizing squared prediction error — closed-form least squares for ARX models, iterated Gauss–Newton for ARMAX/OE/BJ, one-shot linear algebra (projection + SVD) for subspace/state-space models, all with a recursive variant for online use — (3) supplying an input rich enough (persistent excitation) that the parameters are identifiable, and (4) validating that nothing predictable is left in the residuals, on data the model has never seen.
